item.title: Leveraging deep generative modelling at the agent level in discrete-event simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.07995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emulators are often invoked to facilitate parameter inference in computationally intensive agent-based simulations (ABSs). Most approaches, however, require a large sample of pre-existing outputs on which such emulators can be trained. For computationally intensive simulations, this sample can be prohibitively expensive to generate. We propose a new approach to leverage emulators at the agent level in event-based ABSs to reduce the computational requirements of the simulation itself. We demonstrate this in a computationally intensive ``multi-disease'' ABS, Thanzi La Onse, which self-consistently simulates a wide range of medical conditions in a population. By applying conditional tabular generative adversarial networks to replace the modelling of one of the simulated causes of ill health, road traffic injuries (RTIs), we are able to improve its simulation run-time by 86.6% (95% bootstrap confidence interval [85.2, 88.1]), while recovering the evolution of cause-specific mean disability adjusted life years with a 13% error, despite the low assumed incidence of fatal RTIs (~2%). Crucially, we do so while retaining the full ABS framework, and correctly recovering multi-disease dynamics. This represents a crucial step towards enabling full-model emulators for very computationally intensive simulations, and making large ABS amenable to rigorous parameter inference and a full understanding of parameter sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Margherita Molaro, Matthew M. Graham, Oliver Watson, Rachel E. Murray-Watson, Martin Chalkley, Joseph H. Collins, Bingling She, Asif U. Tamuri, Timothy B. Hallett

item.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.05849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction's reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder's reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Zheyu Zhang, Yuanhao Huang, Fan Feng, Jie Liu

item.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.07265v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $\theta$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
item.dc:creator: Achille Raviez, Lan Wang, Brendan Delaney

item.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.07653v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.
item.dc:creator: Haichuan Tan, Bowen Gao, Tao Huang, Jiaxin Tan, Xin Hong, Baoguo Yao, Yifei Wang, Zhichao Deng, Hanji Du, Dapeng Jiang, Yiheng Li, Weiwei Ma, Xin Ma, Yuqi Shi, Zixiang Wang, Kelin Wu, Tianxiang Wu, Wenxuan Xie, Jie Zang, Huiyu Zhang, Mojia Zhang, Yuying Zhang, Ya-Qin Zhang, Wei-Ying Ma, Yanyan Lan

item.title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
item.description: arXiv:2611.08215v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.
item.dc:creator: Federico Dimatz, Marcelo N Kuperman

item.title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2611.08314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.
item.dc:creator: Timon S. Gutleb

item.title: scTREAT: Latent Diffusion for Single-Cell Drug-Response Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2510.11726v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generating drug-induced transcriptional responses requires a model to account for cellular background together with molecular identity and dose. We present scTREAT, the first diffusion framework to factorize state and drug guidance for single-cell drug-response prediction. A shared latent expression space connects baseline and response, while Guided Decomposable Attention (GD-Attn) injects a baseline representation and a dose-conditioned molecular embedding. Independent channel dropout exposes four conditioning states during training; inference combines three conditional predictions with separately specified state and drug coefficients, and dose modulates drug-guidance strength. On condition-level pseudobulk profiles derived from the Tahoe-100M single-cell atlas, scTREAT achieves the best value on 10 of 12 metrics for unseen cell line-drug combinations (UC) and 11 of 12 for unseen drugs (UD). Ablations examine condition injection, molecular representation, and guidance design. On UD, the relative gains over the second-best model reach 36.11% and 34.21% for DEG logFC-Spearman and logFC-Pearson. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining shared latent expression modeling with explicit state and drug conditioning for response prediction.
item.dc:creator: Zhaokang Liang, Shuyang Zhuang, Xiaoran Jiao, Weian Mao, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen

item.title: scDNM-VAE enables directly inspectable deep clustering of single-cell RNA-seq data through signed dendritic gating
item.description: arXiv:2608.17228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep clustering models for single-cell RNA sequencing often assign cells through latent or centroid-based mechanisms that are difficult to inspect. We introduce scDNM-VAE (single-cell Dendritic Neuron Model Variational Autoencoder), a deep clustering framework that combines a variational autoencoder with a dendritic neuron-inspired head. Cluster assignments are governed by learnable signed synaptic weights and thresholds: the weight sign determines the direction of a gate's response to a latent coordinate, its magnitude controls steepness, and the weight-threshold pair determines the transition location. The trained clustering function can therefore be inspected directly without fitting a post-hoc explanation model. We benchmark scDNM-VAE on four datasets spanning immune, cortical, cardiac, and hematopoietic cells against scVI followed by KMeans and an MLP-DEC ablation. scDNM-VAE performs better than scVI on PBMC3k, comparably on the Human Heart Cell Atlas and Paul15, and worse on Zeisel, while producing biologically coherent marker-gene signatures. Ablating each cluster's three highest-magnitude synaptic dimensions causes numerically greater reassignment than random-dimension ablation across all datasets, but the margins are modest and negligible on Zeisel. These results show that signed dendritic gating supports competitive clustering with a parameter-inspectable decision function, while indicating that decision-relevant information is distributed across the latent space.
item.dc:creator: Melih Agraz, Deniz Karapinar, Aysel Topsir, Qianying Cao, Erol Egrioglu, Gaurav Choudhary
